stack/one: A photo becomes a vector by laying all its numbers out in one row, pixel after pixel. Pressing a grid of pixels into a single row like this is called flattening.
stack/many: But a program rarely has just one photo. Flatten four, and stack their rows one under another.
stack/line: Now the numbers line up. Read across a row, and you get one photo. Read down a column, and you get the same number from every photo: here, each one's top left red.
stack/matrix: A grid of numbers in rows and columns like this is called a matrix.
stack/name: The English mathematician James Joseph Sylvester named it, in 1850. Matrix is Latin for womb, or source: he saw it as the grid that smaller, square grids are drawn from, by picking a few of its rows and as many of its columns.
stack/W: Matrices are usually named with capital letters, so call this one W.
stack/shape: Its shape is its size: how many rows, then how many columns, always in that order. Four photos of forty eight numbers each make it four by forty eight.
stack/big: A real stack is bigger. Ten flattened thirty two by thirty two color photos, of three thousand and seventy two numbers each, make a ten by three thousand and seventy two matrix.
grid/rows: To read one up close, take a small W. Count its rows, top to bottom: two.
grid/cols: Count its columns, left to right: three.
grid/shape: So its shape is two by three. NumPy writes it two, three, in round brackets, rows first.
grid/size: Every row holds one number for each column, so W holds two times three: six numbers. Rows times columns, not rows plus columns.
grid/back: It works backward too. Six numbers in two rows means six over two, three, in each row: three columns.
index/ij: To pick out one entry, give its row, then its column, in square brackets. Like a vector's entries, both count from zero.
index/photo: Row first, as in the shape. In the stack of photos, the row picks the photo, and the column picks which of its numbers.
index/eg: W of zero, two is in row zero, the first, and column two, the third: it is two.
index/eg2: W of one, zero is in the second row and the first column: zero. Swap the two numbers, and you ask for a different entry.
index/last: With two rows and three columns, the last entry is W of one, two: each index is one less than its count.
index/out: So W of two, zero does not exist. The rows are numbered zero and one, and there is no row two.
transpose/flip: Sometimes a matrix is wanted the other way round. Stand each row of W up, and lay it down as a column.
transpose/name: This is called transposing, from the Latin for putting across: rows and columns trade places.
transpose/cayley: Arthur Cayley set it out in 1858, in his memoir on the theory of matrices. Transposing, he wrote, turns a broad matrix into a deep one.
transpose/sym: The transpose of W is written W transpose, with a small raised T. In code, it is W dot T.
transpose/shape: Two rows of three become three rows of two, so W transpose has shape three by two: the two numbers of the shape swap.
transpose/ij: Each entry's two indices swap too. The five at W of one, two lands at W transpose of two, one.
